This walks through the pipeline from a standing start: what to install, what your
data has to look like, what to change, and how to read each part's output. Code
here is for copying — none of it executes when the site builds.

## 1. What you need

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
### Prerequisites

R 4.2 or later, and RStudio if you want the point-and-click render button. A full
run takes a few hours the first time, mostly BART sampling; afterwards caching
makes re-runs take seconds.
:::

```r
## CRAN packages
install.packages(c("BART", "dbarts", "bartMan", "caret", "rpart", "rpart.plot",
                   "ggplot2", "dplyr", "tidyr", "purrr", "ggh4x", "gridExtra",
                   "scales", "bcf", "xgboost", "grf", "extraDistr", "devtools"))

## RIQITE is not on CRAN — it provides the randomization-inference engine
devtools::install_github("li-xinran/RIQITE")
```

Two source files sit next to the `.Rmd` and are loaded by it:

| File | What it provides |
|---|---|
| `clusterfunctions.R` | `lbart.cluster()` and `wbart.cluster()` — run several BART chains in parallel and collect them into one posterior |
| `helper_functions.R` | `method_combine()` and the rest of the ITE-quantile machinery, from the [paper's repository](https://github.com/Zhe-Chen-1999/Enhanced_inference_for_ITE_quantiles) |

## 2. What your data has to look like

One row per randomized patient, no missing values in the analysis variables:

| Object | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `y` | numeric | the outcome — `0/1` for binary, any numeric for continuous |
| `z` | **logical** | treatment assignment, `TRUE` = treated |
| `X` | data.frame | baseline covariates; factors stay factors |

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
`z` must be **logical**, not numeric `0/1`. Several helpers use it as a mask —
`mean(y[z])` — and a numeric `z` would index *positionally* instead, silently
computing the wrong thing rather than erroring.
:::

```r
X <- dat[, c("age", "sofa_score", "comorbidity", "lives_at_home")]
y <- dat$death_28d          # 0/1
z <- dat$arm == "treatment"  # logical
```

## 3. The one block you edit

Everything downstream is driven by a single configuration chunk:

```r
OUTCOME_TYPE <- "binary"    # "binary" or "continuous"
GLOBAL_SEED  <- 123
CACHE_DIR    <- "cache"
REFRESH_ALL  <- FALSE       # TRUE forces every cached result to recompute

## Part IV: randomization-based inference
ALPHA <- 0.1                # 1 - ALPHA confidence
NPERM <- 1e4                # permutation draws

## Which parts to run
RUN_PRIOR_GRID    <- TRUE
RUN_CROSS_METHOD  <- TRUE
RUN_BASELINE_RISK <- TRUE
```

`OUTCOME_TYPE` switches the whole document: logistic vs. standard BART, the
XGBoost objective, the prognostic-model family, and every axis label. Set the
three `RUN_*` flags to `FALSE` while drafting to keep re-renders quick.

### How the cache works

A full run takes hours, almost all of it BART sampling. Nobody will iterate on
prose if every re-knit costs an afternoon, so each expensive result is wrapped in
a small helper:

```r
step1.res <- cached("step1_bart_binary", {
  bart_fit_binary_outcome(X, y, z, ...)     # only runs if the file is absent
})
```

The first time through, the block runs and the result is written to
`cache/step1_bart_binary.rds`. Every later knit finds that file and reloads it in
milliseconds. A second knit of the whole document takes seconds rather than
hours, so you can edit text freely.

The appendix prints a table of what was computed and what was reloaded on that
run, so you can always tell which is which.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
### The one thing to watch

**The cache is keyed on the name, not on the inputs.** It has no idea what went
into producing the result. Change your data, a seed, or a hyperparameter and the
*old* result is silently reloaded — no error, no warning, just stale numbers
under a new label.

So after any such change, set `REFRESH_ALL <- TRUE`, knit once, then set it back
to `FALSE`.
:::

To recompute just one thing rather than everything, delete that single file:

```bash
rm cache/step1_bart_binary.rds     # this one recomputes; everything else reloads
```

And if you change an analysis in a way that makes the old result meaningless —
a different estimator, a different analysis set — give it a **new name** rather
than reusing the old one. That makes the stale file impossible to load by
accident:

```r
ci_two <- cached("ite_twosided_m2", { ... })   # renamed from ite_twosided
```

## 4. Part I — who benefits, and which covariates say so

**Stage 1** fits BART to the outcome and returns a posterior CATE for every
patient:

```r
step1.res <- bart_fit_binary_outcome(
  X, y, z,
  Power  = 3, Base = 0.25, Ntrees = 50,   # selected by 10-fold CV
  seed = GLOBAL_SEED, nchains = 4,
  ndpost = 1000, nskip = 500
)
cate.res <- step1.res$cate_results
```

Passing vectors instead of scalars for `Power`/`Base`/`Ntrees` triggers the
cross-validation search — budget over two hours for that.

**Stage 2** fits a regression tree *to* those estimates, which is where the
interpretable subgroups come from:

```r
cart_fit(point_est = cate.res$cate,
         posterior = step1.res$cate_posterior,
         X = X_unscaled, metric = EFFECT_LABEL,
         maxdepth = 3, cp = 0.01)
```

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
The tree's splits are **hypotheses about effect modification**, not tested
subgroup effects. There is no multiplicity control here, and a single CART is
unstable — perturb the data slightly and a split can flip.
:::

## 5. Part II — is the picture real?

Four independent checks on Part I, each trying to break it:

- **MCMC diagnostics** — autocorrelation and Geweke statistics. Slow decay means
  raise `BART_KEEPEVERY`.
- **VIVI heatmaps** — which covariates and *interactions* the ensemble actually
  used. The diagonal is a posterior split-inclusion proportion; the off-diagonal
  is interaction strength, which a CART barplot structurally cannot show.
- **Prior grid** — eight BART prior configurations. If the shrinkage ratio stays
  near zero across all of them, the posterior cannot separate patients and any
  apparent subgroup structure is fragile.
- **Cross-method comparison** — Bayesian Causal Forest and XGBoost T-/S-learners
  on the same data.

## 6. Part III — is it just baseline risk?

Effect heterogeneity often tracks a patient's overall prognosis rather than any
specific covariate. A prognostic score is estimated three ways — control-arm
only, full-sample without the treatment indicator, and sample-split — patients
are grouped into quartiles, and the treatment effect is reported within each.

Comparing the three guards against the score itself being an artifact of how it
was fitted.

## 7. Part IV — what fraction actually benefit?

This is the part with no outcome model. It asks a question Parts I–III cannot
answer, using only the randomization.

```r
## Shuffle first: the rank statistic breaks ties by index order
set.seed(GLOBAL_SEED)
ord <- sample(length(z))
Z <- as.numeric(z)[ord]; Y <- as.numeric(y_cont)[ord]; n <- length(Z)

## One-sided lower confidence limits for every effect quantile
ci_lower <- method_combine(
  Z = Z, Y = Y, N = n, k_vec = 1:n,
  alpha = ALPHA, simul = TRUE, nperm = NPERM,
  treat.method.list   = list(name = "Stephenson", s = 6),
  control.method.list = list(name = "Stephenson", s = 6)
)

plot_quantile_lower(ci_lower$lower)
```

Upper limits come from re-running with the treatment labels switched, then
negating and reversing:

```r
ub <- method_combine(Z = 1 - Z, Y = Y, N = n, k_vec = 1:n,
                     alpha = ALPHA, simul = TRUE, nperm = NPERM,
                     treat.method.list   = list(name = "Stephenson", s = 6),
                     control.method.list = list(name = "Stephenson", s = 6))
upper <- -ub$lower[n:1]
```

### Turning limits into a count

If the lower limit satisfies $L_k > c$ then $\tau_{(k)} > c$, and because the
effects are sorted, so does every larger one — hence *at least* $n - k + 1$
patients have an effect above $c$:

```r
n_benefit <- sapply(thresholds, function(cc) {
  kk <- which(ci_lower$lower > cc)
  if (length(kk)) n - min(kk) + 1L else 0L
})
```

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
### Read the direction from the right limit

If a **larger outcome is good**, benefit is $\tau_i > c$ — read it from the
**lower** limits. If a **larger outcome is bad** (mortality, more disability),
benefit is $\tau_i < c$ — read it from the **upper** limits.

Spend the whole of $\alpha$ on the direction you care about. Reading one side off
a two-sided interval uses $\alpha/2$ and is needlessly conservative.
:::

## 8. Interpreting the whole thing

| Parts I–III say | Part IV says | Conclusion |
|---|---|---|
| covariate-driven HTE | benefiting fraction certified | Strongest case — report the subgroup tree and the bounds together |
| covariate-driven HTE | bounds uninformative | Common in small trials. Lead with the subgroup finding; note the model-free bound neither confirms nor contradicts it |
| flat CATE surface | benefiting fraction certified | Real heterogeneity, **not** explained by measured covariates. Do not report "no HTE" |
| flat CATE surface | bounds uninformative | The honest null. **Not** evidence of a constant treatment effect |

Three things to carry into any write-up:

1. **State the estimand as bounds, never as a point.** "With 90% confidence, at
   least X% of patients benefited" — not "X% benefited".
2. **Never report a flat CATE surface as homogeneity.**
3. **Report the shuffle seed and the rank score.** Ties are broken by index
   order, so discrete-outcome results depend on both.
